A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages A study of non-verbal communication carried out in 1967 continues to be widely quoted today. David Lapakko looks at limitations in the original study Description of the Study The findings of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages in communication by Albert Mehrabian and his colleagues at UCLA' in 1967 have been quoted so frequently that they are now often regarded as a self-evident truth In the first subjects were asked to listen to a recording of a female saying the word 'maybe' in three tones of voice to convey liking, neutrality and disliking. The subjects were then shown photos of female faces expressing the same three emotions and were asked to guess the in the recorded voice and the photos. It was found that the photos got more accurate than the voices. In the second experment. subjects listened to nine recorded words in different tones of voice. Three words had positive meanings (e.g. honey). three were neutral (e.g. Oh) and three were negative (e.g. temble). Again, the subjects had to guess the speaker's emotions. It was found that tone Of voice carried more meaning than the individual words. From these experiments the researchers concluded that 7% of our feeling towards a is based on the actual words they use. 38% on their tone of voice, and 55% on their body language (e.g. facial expression). Methodological Issues However. a closer look at the study reveals several limitations. The first is that the entire study involved only 62 subjects. Of these, 25 were used to select the word for the first experiment, while the key issue — comparing verbal and non-verbal communication — was determined by only the 37 remaining subjects All were female undergraduates who participated as part of their introductory psychology course, and their ages and academic qualifications seem remarkably uniform. Thus, the findings may simply a product of the nature of the sample. Critics have also pointed out that the 7-38-55 formula is flawed sinæ it was pecæd from two different excwiments, neither of which involved all three channels (verbal, vocal, and facial). In addition, in the first the single word maybe was used throughout so it was impossible for the effeds of changes in verbal input to be assessed The researchers intentionally used a 'neutral' word so naturally the subjects found little meaning there. Clearly, such a methodology lacks validity. In the real world, communicate in a particular context and speak in phrases and full-blown sentences, making extensive uæ of the vehicle of My concern is that interpretations of this study have gained such prominence in our #dagogical literature. This 7-38-55 formula apgEars in many basic texts, used for training in public speaking, interpersonal communication and organizational communication.

• UCLA. University of California at Los

10

Lessons to consider

Clearly, one aspect of the Mehrabian study is its numerical precision. Communication is a complex phenomenon, but it seems less when we can rely on these three magical numbers. In contrast to the ambiguities of language, numbers seem to possess exactness. And the popular appeal of the study has given the 7-38-55 formula enormous credibility. There is a certain mystique about non-verbal communication, and the continued references to this research sustain it, encouraging to tEIieve in the overwhelming importance of the non-verbal message compared with the verbal one. Yet we know that even one ill-chosen word to a colleague or friend can make or break a communicative effort. Words do matter. (1991), one Of the few writers to criticize the Mehrabian study, makes the same when he observes, 'If we could communicate 93% of information and attitudes with vocal and facial cues, it would be wasteful to time learning a language' Mehrabian himself his research should not be interpreted to devalue the role of language in communication, saying:

Please remember that my findings.. dealt with communications of feelings and attitudes... it is absurd to imply or suggest that the verbal portion of all communication constitutes only 7% ot the message... anytime we abstract relationships (e.g., x = y — tne square of z) clearly 100% of the entire communication is verbal. (Mehrabian, 1995) To be fair. many textbook writers attempt to be faithful to the context of Mehrabian's research. For example, Stewart and D'Angelo (1988) write: 'Mehrabian argues that when we're uncertain about what someone's feeling, or about how much we like him or her, we rely. . only 7% on the words that are sgx)ken'. Others try to play down the specific percentages, saying tnat an understanding of the general ot non-verbal cues iS more important. Nonetheless, other textbOOk authors simply use the numtErs without placing any limits on their meaning Conclusion Since this relatively small study was first published it has achieved an influence far its intended scope. We need to put it into its proper pers*ctive and learn some important lessons from it regarding social science research, communication pedagogy, and the foræs which have created widespread misunderstanding about communication.
